column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the description (parentage, one daughter, the purchase of the CSS Shenandoah, a plant genus)

The entry says he defeated Pyrrhus near Beneventum; the article calls the battle inconclusive but says it forced Pyrrhus out of Italy. I gave only the outcome, without calling it a victory or a draw. The article says 'ending the Samnite War'; the entry says the Third Samnite War. Not repeated.
Article gives a measles epidemic of 1908, the suicides of his sons and Prince Wilhelm of Sweden's description of 1920; left out for length.
'Reign' used because the entry calls him despot ruling the province; if the editor prefers, 'Career' could absorb it. Article: died 10 April 1380 at Mistra; consistent with entry dates c. 1326–1380.

Entry: residence 'from the thirteenth century to 1719' and 'rebuilt as a Baroque fortress' after 1631. The article gives the court's move as 1719/20 and calls the post-1631 rebuilding a Baroque residence; I avoided both the year of the move and the description of the rebuilding.
Article gives birth 'between 1260 and 1265'; entry says c. 1260. Not stated in the text.
The article does not mention the Medulli; nothing added about them.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it also says some Egyptologists (Jürgen von Beckerath) place him late in the 10th Dynasty rather than as founder of the 9th, as the entry has him, and dates his reign either from c. 2160 BCE or about a century later
The article says it was commissioned in 1180 and copied between 1186 and 1190; the entry's c. 1180–1190 covers both, but I did not repeat the dates.

Entry says he founded Essaouira; the article says he 'developed' the present city in 1769 and also lists Mogador among towns he rebuilt after 1755. I wrote 'developed Essaouira in 1769', which does not contradict 'founded'. Left out the harem and the disputed Helen Gloag story.
Article romanizes the general as Kang Cho; the entry has Gang Jo. I used Kang Cho, as the checker reads the article.
The article says nothing of the Taíno crossings or the chiefdom of Higüey named in the entry; nothing added about them.
Article says the Order purchased the land in 1220 (entry: acquired 1220), consistent; the castle's own article heading gives building 1228–1271. Not stated.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the description it gives only the length (about 50 km), the crest height and the modern D1 highway and 1847 railway
The entry places the Panionion on the slopes; the article says on the north side of the mountain, found in 2004 on Dilek Daglari, a smaller peak. Consistent.

'Reception and legacy' used as the person headings offer no fit for a figure whose death is not told; change to the person list if the checker refuses it. Article: the Emerald Buddha 'would have been created ... by Nagasena', i.e. by the legend; the 43 BCE date sits oddly with his c. 150 BCE floruit, but both are as the article gives them, the second as legend.
SKIPPED: the article holds little beyond lists of office-holders by legislative period; nothing of substance to add to the description
The article places him in the 16th Dynasty without naming Ryholt; the 17th-Dynasty alternative in the description is not discussed there. Petrie Museum seal numbers left out.
The article spells the throne name both Aasehre and Aahsere; I used Aasehre (the lead's form) once and avoided the other.

The article's lead puts the heartland at 'the eastern end of Lake Ontario', which seems a slip; left out. It gives the last reference to the Neutrals as an independent society both as 1653 and (French records) 1672; left out. The 1651 dispersal is in the description and not repeated.

The article dates the alliance and ousting of Cáceres to 1894 and Piérola's presidency to 1895; the description says the coalition overthrew Cáceres in 1895. I gave no year for the ousting. The article gives no year for the Dreyfus contract (the description has 1869).

The description dates Umar Tall's capture of Nioro to 1854; the article gives 11 April 1855. Neither date printed. The article puts the town in the Nioro Region, the description in the Kayes Region; no region named.
The article attributes the conclusion about the Magi's worldview without a name; I put it with Froyanov's analysis, which is how the article presents it.
The article says the town had 4-5,000 inside the walls in the 15th century but also 'an estimated population of about 40,000' at its fall in 1455; the latter left out as inconsistent.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, most of it a list of marriages and children; too little to add
The article spells the lyricist both Montross and Montrose, as the description does.

The article's lead says Old Dongola was the Makurian capital 'from the fourth to the fourteenth century', but its history section says founded in the fifth century and capital from the mid-sixth; I followed the history section, which agrees with the description. Throne Hall's conversion (1317) is in the description and not repeated.
The article says Hoffmann announced the end of the ceasefire 'in two-days time on 17 February'; the wording is unclear, so no date given for the end of the ceasefire.
Article is short (about 330 words); nothing on Srivijaya beyond the description's point.
SKIPPED: the article's history is three short paragraphs; the rest is lists of classes and recipients
The article calls the 821 envoy 'from the Samanid Empire', which looks anachronistic; kept as given, but the editor may wish to drop the attribution.

The article mentions Haubrichs's identification of a presbyter Otfridus who died on 23 January 867, which would contradict the description's 'after 870'; left out. The article spells the archbishop both Luitbert and Liutbert; I used Luitbert.

The description says he introduced Lutheranism in Neuburg in 1542; the article says he converted in 1541 and the chapel was consecrated in 1543. No conversion year printed. The Ottheinrich Building at Heidelberg is not in the article.
Length 459 km in the article; the description's 'about 460 km' agrees, so not repeated.

The entry dates Juvarra's facade 1718-1721; the article says he designed it in 1716 and works halted in 1721. The start date is left out. The article calls the palace the first Senate of the Kingdom of Italy in its lead but the Subalpine Senate in its history; only the latter is used.

The article's claim that Panglao has more marine biodiversity than Japan and the Mediterranean is left out as a comparison. History in the article is very short; the Bo-ol and Dapitan sentence is as the article gives it.

The article calls the Limousin Peace of God (994-1032/3) largely fictitious, an account by Ademar of Chabannes; left out for length. The article's 'ferial days' as consecrated times under the Peace is left out as unclear.
The entry calls Castilla de Oro the governorship; the article says governor of Panama (1514-1526). Used neither title beyond what is consistent.

The article's lead says minister of justice, the body says Minister of the Interior; the text says only 'a minister', as the entry says chief minister. The Pacte Rossi is described as a revised constitution; 'Swiss' follows the diet of 1832 context; could be read as cantonal. Editor may prefer 'revised constitution'.
The article is short; the text adds Fulvia's role, the course of the campaign and the altars of Perusia. The entry's burning of the city is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article says Peter reigned as duke 1213-1221 and was regent 1221-1237; the entry's 'ruled 1213 to 1237' is consistent and the text follows that split. The article says he died at sea 'before he was able to return home'; 'on the way home' is that statement.
The historian named Roman Solanchyk in the article is probably Roman Solchanyk; not used.
The article says the Sultan named 'Pierrakos' bey in 1814, meaning Petros of the Pierrakos family; the text says him. The article calls the islands the Heptanese; kept as the Heptanese.

The entry places Kulen about 40 km north-east of Angkor; the article says 30 km north of Angkor Wat and 48 km north of Siem Reap. No distance is given in the text. The article dates the Devaraja cult to 804 CE while the entry places the ceremony in 802; the cult is given without a date. The article calls Preah Ang Thom's Buddha both 'giant reclining' and 'a large statue' 8 m high; the text keeps both facts as given.
The 'failure of Sir James Keating' episode is left out for length.

The entry calls the society the Accademia dei Pugni; the article Società dei Pugni. Used the article's name as another name of the same body. The article's list of Verri's influences names six people while calling them four; Gibbon left out.

The entry says the amendment was abrogated in 1934; the article says most provisions were repealed in 1934 and that the 1934 treaty dropped three of the seven pledges. The text says only that the 1934 treaty replaced that of 1903 and that the 1940 convention removed it from the constitution.

The entry gives his birth as c. 1743; the article as c. 1753. No birth year is given in the text. The article also says he succeeded his father as Ari'i-rahi of Porionu'u on 23 November 1802, which conflicts with his rule from 1788; left out.

The entry gives his birth as c. 1774, the article c. 1782; no birth year in the text. The entry speaks of marriage links to the ruling family of Huahine; the article names marriages into the family of Tamatoa III of Raiatea and says the ruler of Huahine first recognised him as sovereign. Both are compatible, but the editor may wish to check the entry's Huahine wording. The article calls the battle Te Feipī; the entry Fei Pi.
The article is short (about 470 words); the text adds the formation, constitution and later fate. The entry's mention of Carrara marble is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article is short (about 380 words); the text gives the territories, the names of the state and its end.
The article does not name Qabus ibn Vushmgir; nothing about the title's origin is added.
The article does not mention the Ninth Legion's move to York; not repeated. The final judgement is Tacitus's as quoted through the 1911 Britannica in the article.

The article dates the republican constitution 1843 in its lead and 1842 in its body; no year is given. Garibaldi joined the rebels in 1836 per the body; the coastal campaign is dated 1839 in the lead. Only the 1839 Laguna date is used.

The article gives the 717 battle as both Vincy (21 March 717) and Vinchy; the entry says Vinchy. The date was left out of the second section to avoid a spelling clash; 'Vinchy' used in Legacy as in the entry.
The article says Abercromby commissioned a townhouse at 66 Queen Street, Edinburgh in both 1791 and 1795; left out.

The article says the temple 'in its current form is believed to have been built during the 17th century', while the entry says the present structure was largely built from the 12th century onward: the dating of the present structure was left out. The article calls the corridor the longest of any Hindu temple; the entry says 'among the longest': the superlative was left out.

The article calls him leader of the 'Nizari Ismaili state and the Order of Assassins', which seems broader than the Syrian branch the entry describes; kept to the Syrian role. The leader who sent him is named Hassan Ala Dhikrihi's Salam, identified with Hassan II.

The article gives several conflicting birth and death years (1433; 1377-1528; 1267-1335); none printed, as the entry dates him to the 15th-16th centuries. Recent politicians' visits to the shrine left out.

The article gives inconsistent dates for the stages: passed by the Reichstag on 24 February 1803, approved by the Delegation on 25 February, ratified by the Reichstag in March, by the emperor on 27 April (or 'the following month'). All exact dates left out.
The article is confused about Shang Zhixin: one passage says he rose in 1674 after his father's death, another that he joined in 1676 (Shang Kexi died 1676). Year of his rising left out.
The article's dates for his directorship start 'after the war'; the entry's 1883 not contradicted.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (background on Armenian migration, two short paragraphs on his life) and adds little to the entry
The papal envoy Possevino's population figures for Moscow (30,000 in 1580) left out for brevity.

The entry says Sadeq Khan was overthrown and killed by Ali Murad Khan; the article says the cause of his death is not known, only that Ali-Morad succeeded him. Manner of death left out. The entry says he governed Basra until 1779; the article only says his forces abandoned it after Karim Khan's death.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the entry (Communist University of the Toilers of the East, 1932 replacement of Donduk Kuular, marriage to Khertek Anchimaa)

The article is inconsistent on her journeys to England ('another two times' vs 'four different occasions'): 'four times in all' used. The article says she was 'forced to marry'; worded 'pressed into the match'. Chatham vs Gillingham for Palm Cottage: Gillingham used as in the fuller passage.

The article gives two birth dates (20 October 1866 in the lead; 'some time in 1868' in the body; entry 1868) and two death dates (17 November and 9 November 1914). Exact dates left out. The entry calls him a former horse dealer; the article does not mention this.
The article says both that Masjid Pekan Seria was rebuilt in 1953 and that it was built in 1954; left out.
Entry spells the name Sese; the article Ssese. Ssese used as in the article (it is also an aka of the entry). The entry's sleeping-sickness sentence is not in the article.

The article names the birthplace both as Qara Rud village and as Garmrood village; neither name is printed. The article says he started writing the Sharafnama in 1597 and also that it was written in 1597; the entry says completed in 1597. The text gives no year for the writing. Death given as c. 1603-04 in the article, c. 1603 in the entry; not repeated.
The article does not mention Mapungubwe's kingdom, only the conservation area.
The article gives him as died c. 1450 BC; the entry as reigned c. 1450 BCE. No year printed.

The article calls James Bruce 'English'; his nationality is left out. The article places the great market in the 'medieval period' section, while the entry dates it to the 18th and early 19th centuries; the text uses only the dated visits of 1772 and 1814. The article spells Burckhardt 'John Ludwik'; only the surname is printed.

The article names the crown prince both Shi Daya and Shi Hong (石弘), and a second son Shi Hong (石宏) Prince of Qin; only the Prince of Qin is named in the text. Death date 17 August 333 is in the lead, but only the year is used.
The article gives his death as 13 January 1527 in the lead and as 1526 in the body; the entry says 1527. No year is printed.

The article's lead dates his appointment over southern Epirus and Acarnania to 1347, its body to 'by 1348'; no year printed. The article pairs 'John Spata and Peter Losha' with 'Arta and Angelokastron', which reads the reverse of the entry; not repeated.
The article gives either Pedro Afonso de Aguiar or Vasco da Gama as leader of the 1502 ships; no name printed. The Ophir and Tarshish identifications (both discarded) left out for length.
The article's lead says 'Through the 5th and 7th centuries'; the entry dates the clan's power to the 6th and 7th; no span printed.
Native Life's description and 'Shakespeare into Tswana' are in the entry and not repeated at length.

The article dates the first Dominican fort to 1562 (burned in 1563, then rebuilt); the entry says 1566. No year printed. The article's account of the Dutch in 1636 is muddled ('the Portuguese were attacked by the Dutch and had to abandon the fort'); worded as the Dutch taking it.

The entry says destroyed in 397 BCE; the article says betrayed and destroyed in 396 BC. No year printed. The article dates the foundation to the 6th century BC in its lead and to the 8th or 7th century BC (after Thucydides) in its history; no date printed.
The article says the headquarters was first in Tokyo and moved to Dalian in 1907; consistent with the entry, not repeated.
The article's 'Ancient period' paragraph (Parmar Rajputs, invasions 95 BC to 846 AD) is unsourced and confused; left out.

The article says Srinagar was under Gorkha rule from 1806 to 1815, while the entry dates the Gorkha conquest to 1804 (the article has the Raja killed in January 1804); the 1806 span is not printed. The article does not date the Gohna Lake dam-burst or say whether it was the 1894 flood; the two are kept apart.

The article's lead gives 1551 for Warmia but its body says 'two years later' after the 1550 consecration; no year printed. The article says Pope Paul IV summoned him to Rome in 1558 and also that he was legate in Vienna from 1558, then 'the following year' Pius IV sent him; no year printed for the nunciature. No date for Braunsberg in the article; the entry's 1564 is not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, mostly a family list; too little to add 260 words without padding

The article is inconsistent on the Rama III years (monk for nearly 20 years; also 'became a monk, but later became a merchant'); the merchant episode is left out. The article names his last patron as Prince Chuthamani (Krom Khun Isaret Rangsan) and as viceroy Pinklao; no name printed.
The article says 14 Remonstrants were summoned and 'thirteen Remonstrant ministers, including Episcopius' were held at Dort; only the fourteen summoned are mentioned.
The entry says the range rises to about 1,500 m; the article gives 1,562 m for Nabi Yunis, which is consistent.
The entry dates the shamkhals' seat at Tarki from the 17th century; the article says Tarki was the Kumyk capital at least from the 16th century. Neither start date is given in the text.

The article gives both 1915 and 1916 for the family's move to the United States; no year is given. The posthumous Maya History is dated 1994 in the text and 1993 in the bibliography; no year is given. Morley's first name is spelled both Silvanus and Sylvanus in the article.
Short article (about 300 words of substance); two sections only. The entry gives his reign as c. 768–777, the article as 768–777.
The article places the sanctuary both on the eastern side and at the north-east point of the island; the text says eastern side.
The entry mentions Pliny the Elder and the Chauci; the article does not, so nothing is said of them. The article's 'Kreis Norfriesland' spelling is taken as Nordfriesland.
The entry's revolt against Roman taxation is not in the article and is not mentioned. Short article; the list of sees fills the last section. 'Legacy' is used as for a state or region.

The entry says he was crowned in April 1736; the article gives his landing in March 1736 and no month for the coronation, so only the landing is dated. The entry says he died 'there' after the debtors' prison; the article has him released in 1755 and dying in London in 1756. Both are kept in the text as the article has them; 'there' in the entry can be read as London.
The article's dates for Calderón's torture (1801) and the trials are used as given; the entry gives no dates for them.

The entry calls him deputy people's commissar for military affairs; the article's lead gives Deputy People's Commissar of War and Commissar of Public Education, while its body says he was made People's Commissar for Military Affairs. No office is named in the text. The article also gives an odd date order for Böhm's order (end of April) and Szamuely's continued tribunals in May; no month is given for the order.
The article dates Aculnahuacatl Tzaqualcatl's rule both to c. 1427 and to his death c. 1430, and Totoquihuaztli I to c. 1428; no dates are given for them.

The entry dates his death to 726, the article to c. 726; no year of death is given in the text. The article places his birth near the Tuul River in the land of the Ashide, while the inscription it quotes says he was born in Tabgach (Tang China) country; only the inscription's words on Chinese rule are given. The article's claim that E. P. Thompson called him a kingmaker looks doubtful and is left out.

The entry dates him c. 1210–1270; the article reasons that he most likely died in the 1270s and that his name appears on no manuscript after 1286 (probably a slip). No death date is given in the text.

The article's lead says the treaty was signed on 4 March 1816; the entry and Whelpton (quoted in the article) have it initialled in December 1815 and ratified in March 1816. No day is given in the text. The article's August 2026 report that the original papers may be lost is left out.

The article says Russian trade was to go through Viborg and Reval, not Narva, but then says the treaty made Vyborg and Narva the hubs; no ports are named in the text. The article calls Sigismund 'a son of the Polish king John I', apparently a slip for John III of Sweden; the text names no father. The entry places Teusina near Ivangorod; the text says only Ingria.
The article gives two dates for entry into force (25 April 1969 and 22 April 1968); neither is used. Its COPREDAL session dates are garbled and left out.

The article says the city was razed in 1478 when Girindrawardhana defeated Kertabhumi and the capital moved to Daha; the entry says it lost prominence by the early sixteenth century. The date of its fall is left out of the text.

The entry says the capital was built above the eastern shore of Lake Van; the article places the ruins east of the lake and just west of modern Van. The text says only close to the shore. The entry's Sarduri I and c. 840 BCE are not in the article and are not mentioned.
The entry calls Tyburn a village; the article a manor. The entry's Brian O'Rourke is not in the article and not mentioned.
The article gives Ziyad's death as 673 in the lead and 672/673 in the body; left the year out.
Entry names Kerei and Janibek; the article names the first Kazakh khans Jānī Beg and Giray. Did not name them.
Article: reign at least 191 to 232 CE; entry: inscriptions roughly 190 to 230. Left the CE range out. Article dates the year-93 inscription c. 171 or 220 CE; left out.
Article dates Boudica's sack to 61; entry says 60 or 61. Left the year out.

Article says that in 1941 Maček called on party supporters to respect and co-operate with Pavelić's regime, which sits uneasily with the entry's 'refused to collaborate with the Ustaše'; left that call out and kept only his refusals of office.
The entry's statement that Rome absorbed their lands into Gallia Narbonensis from the 120s BCE is not in the article; not touched.

Short article; two sections only. Entry says Germans, Flemings and Frisians; the article names settlers from Holstein, Stormarn, Westphalia and Holland, Dutch and Frisians: no conflict printed. The article does not mention the founding of Lübeck.

Entry says Waldemar defended the Mark against the northern coalition; the article says he was defeated near Gransee in 1316 and lost Stargard and Neubrandenburg. Stated the article's facts without the word 'defended'; editor may wish to revisit the entry.
The article describes the defeat at Elmina in 1478 but its lead calls it the Battle of Guinea; used the body's account.
Entry dates the Hittite sack around 1340 BCE; the article says only 'in the first years of his reign' (c. 1344–1322 BCE). No year printed for the sack.
SKIPPED: article has about 200 words of history; the rest is census figures, transport and a list of notable people
Entry mentions Baranya; not in the article. The article says killings were done by units 'commanded by Mihály Horthy', apparently a slip; left out.

Article gives his birth as 913 (about 913 in the family section), the entry c. 915; the article has him styled Count of the Duchy from 959 and Duke from 962, the entry duke from about 959. Left the birth year and the ducal date out. The article says the son William abdicated to Saint-Cyprien, which reads as the son, not this William; the entry says this William retired to a monastery. Not mentioned in the text.
Article calls the 1543 agreement the Marburg Contract; the entry says Treaty of Marburg. No conflict printed.
The article gives his reign as 889-910 and says he died in 910; the entry has 'c. 910', so no death year is printed.
The article dates the saga to about 1225; the entry has c. 1230. No date is printed.
Entry says he fled to Burma in 1659; the article says he retreated to Kunming in 1658 and 'finally fled into Burma in 1661' (and the lead 'by 1661'). No year of flight is printed.
The eye story is already in the entry and is only alluded to.
The article's lead says he was rehabilitated 'more than half a century later', its body says 1622 (40 years); the entry says 1622, so the 'half a century' phrase is not used.

Ibn 'Idhari dates his death to 1075 or 1076; the entry gives d. 1087, so the alternative date is not printed. The Ghana campaign may have been led by his son Yahya (1076); left out as the entry associates Abu Bakr with pressure on Ghana in general.
The article's lead says the sultanate surrendered in 1904, its body that the sultan capitulated in 1903; the entry says 1903, so no surrender year is printed beyond what the entry gives.
The article gives 800 killed and about 500 imprisoned in the January 1599 assault; the entry says 'several hundred', so no figure is printed.

The article says both that the festival was held on the first day of Nisan and that the Babylonian festival started on 4 Nisan; no day is printed. The claim that it advanced Western civilisation is the article's own unsourced judgement and is left out.

The article's lead says flatly that she killed al-Hadi; its body calls it a rumour, as the entry does. The article gives her birthplace as Jorash near Bisha in one place and Mecca in another; no birthplace is printed beyond what the entry says.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, nearly all of it already in the entry (the Subh al-A'sha, Kahn's judgement, Ibn al-Durayhim)
The entry dates the Nahj al-Balagha to around 1009; the article says it was compiled in the tenth century. Neither date is given in the text.
The article identifies the founding with Cyropolis only as 'probably' and 'may have'; hedged.

The entry says Qasim Razvi led the party in 1946-1948; the article says he was elected leader after Bahadur Yar Jung's death in 1944. The text says only that Bahadur Yar Jung died in 1944, without dating Razvi's leadership. The article spells the name both Rizvi and Razvi; Razvi follows the entry. Left out the article's present-day characterisation ('right-wing', 'pro-partition party') and the current seat tallies.

The entry dates the massacre and her hanging to 1503 and her death to 1503; the article gives her death as c. 1504 and says she was imprisoned and tortured for three months after the 1503 massacre. The text gives no year or length for her imprisonment and death. The entry says the chiefs were burnt at a feast; the article says they were lured into a hut and burned alive. Left without either detail. Martyr's claim that she had Bohechío's wife buried alive was left out as a single hostile report.
The article records the island salvage excavations of the early 1980s without detail; the Suhu governors are left to the entry.

The entry dates the marriage to the 920s or 930s; the article says it likely took place in the mid-930s. No date is given in the text. The entry says the marriage brought Aragon under the Navarrese crown; the article says the County of Aragon had already been brought into the Kingdom of Pamplona under Sancho I. The text says neither.
Left out the article's comparison of the reconcentration camps with Nazi camps and its praise ('brilliantly', comparison with Páez).

The entry places the Aorsi on the steppes from about the 2nd century BCE; the article says they and the Siraces are believed to have migrated in the late 5th century BCE, and that they played a major role from the 1st century BCE. The text gives no date for the migration or their first appearance.
The article gives his death as 26 August 787 in its lead but later says that he and his son Romuald died in 788. The text gives no date for either death.

The entry calls him the first Nabataean king to strike coins; the article says only that he ordered the first silver Nabataean coins. The text says silver coins, without 'first'. Damascus capture date (85 BCE) is in the entry and left out here.
'Each wall is 12 metres high': the article says 'Each 12 m wall', read as height.
Founding: article 176 BCE, entry early 2nd century BCE; no date given. Corbulo: entry 58 CE, article 58-59 CE; no date given.
Left out the 2025 film mentioned in the article.
The article's lead gives his death as 26 September 1573 but also says the clan was destroyed in August 1573 and the siege began in July; no exact day is given in the text.

The article says his supremacy dates from the 8th century BC 'after' a break with Tyre at the time of Himera (480 BC), which is self-contradictory; left out. The etymology section is poorly sourced; only the general Ammon connection is used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance
Article gives birth c. 332 BC and death c. January 257 BC; the entry has d. 257 BCE, consistent.
Leadership list in the article gives Muhammad ibn Lubb d. 899, the narrative 8 October 898; the year of his death is left out. Ibn al-Qutiyya called Muwallad; Albelda 851/2 victory left out.
Article says construction began in 1780 and was completed in 1784; the entry says built from 1784. Both start years left out.
The Bardas Skleros article says Phokas was interned in a monastery; this article says exile on Chios, as the entry does.

Entry says he submitted to Basil in 989; the article says the date of his surrender is disputed and places the meeting with Basil in 991. No surrender year given. Entry says the Buyid court; the article says the Abbasid Caliph's court; I wrote Baghdad only.
Entry says the defeat forced David II into exile in France; the article does not mention this, so it is not repeated.

This Baybars al-Salihi is not the later sultan; the article says he was executed in prison. Entry calls the Khwarazmians allies 'under Baybars'; the article has Baybars commanding the Egyptian army - compatible.
Entry says Mircea held the field; the article says Mircea's army was finally obliged to withdraw and that each army withdrew. Who held the field is left out.
Article calls Salsu part of the 'second campaign' of the Goguryeo-Sui War; the entry calls it Emperor Yang's first invasion. Neither numbering used.
Article gives June 1608 but no place of death.
Entry says Duke of Merania from 1188; the article says he assumed the title by about 1180/82 and connects it with the 1180 deposition of Henry the Lion. No year given for the title in the text.

The article says Nehru 'visited the dam to formally inaugurate it' in early 1954, before the first concrete of 17 November 1955 it also gives; the 1954 inauguration was left out as internally inconsistent. Left out: a June 2026 report that the dam was tilting (one line, unexplained).
The article's lead gives his first premiership as March 1948 to February 1950, its body March 1949 to February 1950; the entry says 1949-1950. The first term's dates are left out.
SKIPPED: article has little substance beyond area and census figures and a list of present-day politicians; nothing on the province's history to add to the entry
